notice.why: Why this page exists: I'm applying to Addvery by doing a GTM engineer's work in public, in one day. This page picks out the parts that touch your role.

grid_intro.heading: A page for each of you
paragraphs: As part of my research into Addvery, I tried to work out who a hire like me would actually need a yes from. I stuck to what's public: Addvery's website and the team's own LinkedIn profiles and posts. I landed on six people.

Each of you would judge a GTM engineer on something different. My guess: growth cares about pipeline, delivery about whether what I build still runs after handover, BI about where the numbers come from, and leadership about whether it pays for itself. So instead of one pitch for everyone, **each of you gets your own page**. (Old marketer habit: one reader per page.)
Honestly, **these are guesses from public information**.

pages.name: Ivana Karhanová
pages.label: Addvery's Chief Growth Officer
pages.title: Chief Growth Officer, Addvery
pages.framing: What Alex Alderman would build for Addvery's growth team, and what he'd need from you to make it real.

opening.before: On your post about the road to 1 billion CZK, I said I might like to help. You replied:
opening.quote: let's find out how to make it possible.

why_now.heading: The road to 1 billion CZK
why_now.how: You're building the sales and marketing team from scratch, and the system under it, with AI agents from day one: CRM upkeep, contact capture, buying signals from job ads and news, and content. The salespeople are being hired now. So now is when the system gets built, before the team that runs on it arrives.
why_now.source: your public LinkedIn posts of 18 and 30 to 31 October 2026, paraphrased.

pages.note: Five times the revenue means a pipeline that holds at five times the deals. Building that is a GTM engineer's job, and I'd like it to be mine, so the salespeople you hire walk into a system that already runs instead of building one between calls. Each demo below is a first version of one piece of it.

demos.why: 36 workflows built from Addvery's own industry pages, in English, Czech and German, each opening with a first message written for its lead.
Prospect research at scale, the feed your job-ad and news signals would run on.
Each starts as 15 minutes of a consultant talking and ends near-final, so their expertise becomes content without eating their week.
Posts in Addvery's own voice, checked and waiting for a person to approve. (I've written hundreds of LinkedIn posts myself, so I have opinions here.)

ask.short: What to build first, when we meet
ask.heading: When we meet, could we start with the piece you'd want working first?
ask.body: If one jumps out before then, send me its number and I'll have that one ready to walk through.

pages.sources: Its facts come only from Addvery's public website, your public job title, and your public posts on the 1 billion CZK goal, including your reply to my comment.

landing.greeting: Hi Ivana. The short version before we meet: you're building a sales and marketing team and the system under it at once, and the system is the part I'd like to build with you. So I guessed your questions and answered them here, with the work behind each one.

concerns.q: You already run 14 agents. What would I add?
concerns.a: Your agents flag a company; I'd build what happens next: a drafted first touch in your approval queue, the booked meeting, the CRM stage, the attribution report.

concerns.q: Can it prove pipeline, or is it theatre?
concerns.a: Nothing here sends. I'd propose a pilot scored in your numbers -- accounts enriched, replies, meetings, MQL to SQL -- and if they don't move, we'll both see it.

concerns.q: Who answers for each agent, and what does it cost?
concerns.a: Every agent in this build has a written spec, an owner and a human approval step. Cost per agent gets logged from day one, so each one earns its keep.

concerns.q: A lot of this runs in Czech.
concerns.a: My Czech is B1 to B2, so I'd start with DACH, Asia and group-level buyers, and Czech copy goes through your review step.

landing.note:
So when you answered my comment on the road to 1 billion CZK with "let's find out how to make it possible", I took you literally and spent 12 hours building my application to Addvery, live. It's in your branding, not mine, for a reason: I don't want there to be a next company.

You're hiring salespeople now. The first place you need to put AI is in your pipeline, so they start with one that already runs. That's the core of this page: **36 workflows, and how each lead finds the right one.** Four ICPs from your own website, in English, Czech and German, three tactics each.

Start with the 3-minute video below. (Honest rough edge: nothing has sent, and the Czech and German still need a native read.)

See you soon.

pages.framing: What Alex Alderman would build for Addvery, seen from the CEO's chair, and what he'd need from you to make it real.
pages.note: You decide whether a GTM engineer earns a seat at Addvery, so here are the economics in two lines. AI pays for itself by cutting labour costs or by growing revenue. I'd point it at revenue, so the whole team grows with it. All I'd need from you is which piece to make real first.

demos.why: 36 workflows built from Addvery's own industry pages, each opening with a message written for its lead: the repeatable part of new business.
An agent that watches the work and reports what changed, so you can see where a project stands without calling a meeting.
Research on prospects at scale, so outreach starts from facts about the account.

ask.heading: Which of these would you want working at Addvery first?
ask.body: One demo number in reply to my LinkedIn message. That's the whole ask.

landing.greeting: Hi Stepan. I could have sent you a CV. Instead I spent one recorded day doing the job in public, since a role like this would need your yes. Here are my guesses at your questions, with the proof linked.

concerns.q: Is this another AI-buzz hire?
concerns.lead: I'd hold myself to your line.
concerns.a: You've said a role at Addvery isn't a ride on the AI buzz. I've spent nine months doing nothing but building with Claude Code, and this site is the result. (Technically still a CV. A very long one, with a live feed.)

concerns.q: Where's something running that others can see?
concerns.a: A dozen agents built this site from one written plan, and every decision is logged in the open.

concerns.q: Can I swim without a lifeguard?
concerns.a: Agents made the easy calls, I made the hard ones, and the log shows which was which. The slowest part was decisions waiting on me.

concerns.q: Czech and work authorisation.
concerns.a: Over a decade in the Czech Republic, long-term residency and a trade licence. My Czech is B1 to B2.

pages.name: Pavel Novak
pages.label: Addvery co-founder, Skygena CEO
pages.title: Co-Founder & Advisor, Addvery · Co-Founder & CEO, Skygena
pages.framing: What Alex Alderman would build for the Addvery group, and what he'd need from you to make it real.
pages.note: From a co-founder's seat, the question is whether something pays off across the group. The pipeline below doesn't have to stop at Addvery: the same profiles and routing could send each lead to the group company that fits it, whether that's consulting, IT, media or production AI. One research layer feeding several pipelines is where the cost starts to make sense, and it's the version I'd build if the group wanted one.

demos.why: 36 workflows, one per customer profile, language and approach, and how a classifier would send each lead to the right one. Point that routing at the group, and each lead goes to the company that fits.
An agent that ran all day on the real build recordings and told the site what to add. Small, but working, and past the pilot stage.
Prospect research at scale, the research layer that routing like this runs on.

ask.heading: Is one of these worth a look for the group?
ask.body: If so, its number is all I need. If none is, that's a useful answer too, and it saves us both a meeting.

landing.greeting: Hi Pavel. What goes into the model? It's the first thing I'd ask anyone doing AI work inside a company, so it's the first thing this page answers. The rest are my guesses at what a co-founder would want settled.

concerns.q: What goes into the model?
concerns.a: No client data in GTM tools, no secrets in prompts or on screen, and this whole build ran that way on camera. (Less thrilling to watch. That's fine.)

concerns.q: Process first, then tools.
concerns.a: Every piece of this build started as a written spec before any agent ran.

concerns.q: Does an AI builder belong at Skygena or at Addvery?
concerns.a: I don't know which it should be, and that's the group's call. The same pipeline could route each lead to whichever group company fits it.

pages.name: Lukáš Marek
pages.label: Addvery co-founder, iMEDIATIC CEO
pages.title: Advisor & Co-founder, Addvery · Co-Founder & CEO, iMEDIATIC
pages.framing: What Alex Alderman would build for the group's marketing work, and what he'd need from you to make it real.
pages.note: iMEDIATIC is the group's media agency, so I looked at what an agency makes for client after client: brand templates, articles from an expert's own words, posts in a company's own voice. I built each one for Addvery, in a way that could be pointed at another brand. I've freelanced for ten years and haven't yet built this inside a company with a real CRM and real IT restrictions. A fixed-scope pilot is the cheapest way for both of us to find out how it holds up there.

demos.why: Five LinkedIn templates in Addvery's brand, taken from its public website. The same method would work from a client's brand.
Posts in a company's own voice, worked out from how it already writes, with checks before anything goes out.
Each starts as 15 minutes of an expert talking and ends near-final. They do the last 10%.

ask.short: The demo that would suit a client
ask.heading: Which of these would you want to see working for an iMEDIATIC client?
ask.body: Name the one, and the pilot gets built around it.

landing.greeting: Hi Lukáš. Nobody should pay for a seat on faith, mine included, so I'm open to starting with a fixed-scope, paid pilot. I've looked at Addvery and iMEDIATIC, and your likely questions are next, with plain answers.

concerns.q: A seat that sits idle is a cost.
concerns.a: I'd shape the pilot like iMEDIATIC's own Health Check, with every deliverable named before it starts. (Ten years of freelancing taught me that one.)

concerns.q: What pipeline has this generated?
concerns.a: Nothing here sends. A pilot would be measured in meetings and pipeline, not in how clever the workflows look.

concerns.q: Czech clients, Czech team.
concerns.lead: B1 to B2, with a native reviewer.
concerns.a: I'd start where English works, and Czech copy gets checked by a native speaker before it goes anywhere.

pages.name: Milos Cerovsky
pages.label: Addvery's Chief Delivery Officer
pages.title: Chief Delivery Officer, Addvery
pages.framing: What Alex Alderman would build for delivery at Addvery, and what he'd need from you to make it real.
pages.note: Whatever a GTM system sells, delivery has to carry. So I ran this hackathon like a small engagement: a written charter, one spec per piece of work, a live page showing where everything stands. (Twelve hours, one very demanding client: me.) The same setup could run beside a client project, and you'd know better than me where it would hold up.

demos.why: An agent that watches the work and tells the project page what changed, so the client sees progress without a status call.
A live picture of a project: every piece of work, its status and what changed, updated as it moves. You're looking at it.
Each starts as 15 minutes of talking. Same route, different input: an end-of-project debrief in, a near-final case study out.

ask.short: Where a live project page helps
ask.heading: Where would a live project page like this help on a client project, and where would it get in the way?
ask.body: The “get in the way” half is the more useful one.

landing.greeting: Hi Milos. I'd expect you to judge this the way you'd judge any engagement: what got delivered, by when, and who answered for it. That's what this page tries to show.

concerns.q: Native Czech or Slovak, and Czech work authorisation.
concerns.a: Over a decade in the Czech Republic, long-term residency and a trade licence; my Czech is B1 to B2. The work I'd do is building systems, which doesn't need native Czech.

concerns.q: Has it run in production?
concerns.lead: This site has, since the build day.
concerns.a: A dozen agents built it from one written plan. A pilot would have one stated deliverable within weeks, your own bar.

concerns.q: Who's accountable for agent output?
concerns.a: Every agent here has a written spec, one owner and a human approval step, and its decisions are logged. (So far the name next to every one of them is mine.)

pages.label: Addvery's Head of BI
pages.title: Head of Business Intelligence, Addvery
pages.framing: What Alex Alderman would build for business intelligence at Addvery, and what he'd need from you to make it real.
pages.note: The report is what says whether a pipeline was worth paying for, right? Addvery connects client funnels from first click to signed contract; the demos below are the first steps of that funnel, pointed at Addvery's own new business. I'd want their numbers landing where your team already works.

demos.why: Prospect data pulled at scale, the first rows of any pipeline report.
36 workflows: four customer profiles × three languages × three approaches, the segments a pipeline report would break down by.
An agent that turns hours of raw recordings into short, structured updates. (Given how much I ramble on camera, that's a real data-cleaning job.)

ask.heading: Where would you want the pipeline's numbers to land?
ask.body: Name the tool or the report, and I'll build to fit it, not the other way round.

landing.greeting: Hi David. Every GTM system I'd build ends up as rows in a report, and at Addvery those rows would feed the data your team owns. So you'd be the one to tell me whether they can be trusted.

concerns.q: Where does the data come from, and is it GDPR-safe?
concerns.a: Every number on the research pages names its source. Minimum data, opt-outs handled. No source, no field.

concerns.q: Am I a data person?
concerns.a: I'm a GTM engineer who came up through B2B marketing. I'd want the pipeline's numbers in the tools your team already uses, built to your standards.

concerns.q: Brno works in Czech.
concerns.a: My Czech is B1 to B2. I'm in Prague, and Brno is a train ride away.
